title: Statistical Description of Data
outcomes: Explain what statistics means in its singular and plural senses, where it is used in economics, management and business, and its limitations.
Distinguish primary from secondary data, choose a suitable method of collecting primary data and scrutinise data for consistency.
Classify data (time series, geographical, qualitative, quantitative) and present them in text, a well-built table or the right diagram.
Build a frequency distribution and work out class limits, boundaries, mid-values, width, frequency density, relative and cumulative frequencies.
Read and draw a histogram, frequency polygon, ogives and frequency curves, and know what each one reveals.

meta.exam_tip: This unit gives quick, almost free marks in Paper 3: definitions (stub, caption, primary data), class boundaries, mid-values, cumulative frequencies and pie-chart angles. Questions are short — do not over-think them, but watch for inclusive vs exclusive classes.

concepts.title: Statistics — the word, its two meanings and its uses
body: The word is traced to the Latin "status", the Italian "statista", the German "statistik" and the French "statistique" — all linked to the state, because early statistics were records kept by rulers. Kautilya's Arthashastra recorded births and deaths; Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari kept agricultural records in Akbar's time.

In the plural sense, statistics means the numbers themselves — figures collected about some characteristic with a view to analysis (e.g. "the GST collection statistics"). In the singular sense, statistics is the science of collecting, organising, analysing and presenting data and then drawing conclusions from them; it is sometimes called the science of counting or the science of averages.

Economics uses it for time series, index numbers, demand analysis, regression-based forecasts and econometrics. Business management uses sampling and decision theory instead of guesswork. Commerce and industry use averages, dispersion, correlation, index numbers and quality control to plan output and maximise profit.
concepts.analogy: Plural "statistics" is the pile of bricks; singular "statistics" is the art of building a house from them.
concepts.work: An auditor who picks 60 vouchers out of 6,000, an analyst forecasting next year's sales, a cost accountant tracking material usage — all of them use statistics every week, even if they never call it that.

concepts.title: Limitations of statistics
body: It studies aggregates. One person's salary is not a statistic; the average salary of 500 employees is.
It works with quantitative data. Qualities (honesty, colour) must first be given numbers or counted before analysis.
Projections hold only under the conditions they assumed. If conditions change, a sales forecast can be badly wrong.
Inference rests on random sampling. A sample picked carelessly gives misleading conclusions — experts should design the sample.
concepts.analogy: Statistics is a wide-angle lens: superb for the crowd, useless for one face in it.
concepts.work: When a client says "your sample did not include my biggest customer", you explain that statistical conclusions are about the population as a whole, and that a carefully designed sample is what makes them reliable.

concepts.title: Collecting data: primary, secondary and scrutiny
body: Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator for the purpose in hand. Secondary data were collected earlier by someone else and are now being reused. The same figures are primary for the collector and secondary for a later user.

Methods of collecting primary data: (i) interview — personal (meet the respondent; accurate, good even after disasters), indirect (ask people connected with the event, e.g. after a rail accident) and telephone (quick, cheap, wide coverage but less consistent); (ii) mailed questionnaire (wide area, but non-response is highest); (iii) observation (measure directly, e.g. heights — most reliable but slow, costly and covers a small area); (iv) questionnaires filled in by enumerators, who meet people and explain the questions — used for large enquiries.

Sources of secondary data: international bodies (WHO, ILO, IMF, World Bank), government publications (CSO's Statistical Abstract, ministry reports), private and quasi-government bodies (ISI, ICAR, NCERT) and unpublished research.

Scrutiny means checking data for accuracy and consistency before using them. There are no fixed rules — the statistician uses intelligence, patience and experience: look for copying errors, test internal consistency (density should equal population ÷ area), spot identical-looking returns from a careless enumerator, and get disputed cases recollected.
concepts.analogy: Primary data are vegetables you grow yourself; secondary data are vegetables from the market — cheaper and quicker, but check them for freshness (scrutiny) before you cook.
concepts.work: In audit, a debtor confirmation you send yourself is primary evidence; the client's own ageing report is secondary. Checking that total sales in the GST returns agree with the books is exactly an internal-consistency check.

concepts.title: Classification of data
body: Classification arranges data into groups or classes of similar items. It condenses the data, makes comparison possible, removes needless detail and is the starting point of any analysis.

Four bases: chronological (temporal / time series — e.g. monthly production for five years); geographical (spatial — e.g. candidates by State); qualitative (by an attribute such as gender or nationality — ICAI also calls it ordinal); quantitative (by a measurable variable such as profit or weight — also called cardinal).
Qualitative and quantitative data are frequency data (we count how many fall in each group). Time series and geographical data are non-frequency data.
concepts.analogy: Sorting a heap of laundry by owner (attribute), by size (variable), by the day it was washed (time) or by the room it goes to (place).
concepts.work: A sales ledger can be classified by month (time series), by branch (geographical), by product type (qualitative) or by invoice size (quantitative). Each view answers a different management question.

concepts.title: Textual and tabular presentation
body: Textual presentation writes the data in paragraphs. It is simple and keeps exact figures, but it is dull and comparison is hard; it is unsuitable for data classified in many ways.

Tabulation arranges data in rows and columns. A good table has: a table number; a self-explanatory title; a caption (the column headings) — the box-head is the whole upper part including column headings, sub-columns, column numbers and units; a stub (the left part describing the rows); the body (the figures); footnotes and the source at the bottom. It should be balanced, show totals and units, and make comparison easy.
Tabulation is preferred to text because it makes comparison easy, handles complicated data, is needed before drawing diagrams and is essential for statistical analysis.
concepts.analogy: A table is like a railway timetable: stations down the left (stub), trains across the top (caption), times in the body.
concepts.work: Every schedule to the financial statements is a statistical table. Partners review whether totals, units ("₹ in lakh") and notes are shown — the same rules as here.

concepts.title: Diagrams: line, bar and pie
body: Diagrams reach even a non-technical audience and reveal hidden trends, but they are less accurate than tables — when precision matters, use a table.

Line diagram (historiagram): plots a time series against time. When values vary over a wide range or we care about rates of growth, use a ratio chart (log chart) — log of the value is plotted. Multiple line chart: two or more related series in the same unit. Multiple-axis chart: related series in different units.

Bar diagrams: horizontal bars for qualitative or spatial data; vertical bars for quantitative or time series data. Multiple (grouped) bars compare related series; component (sub-divided) bars show the parts of a total; percentage bars show each part as a share of 100.
Pie chart (circle diagram): shows the parts of a whole. Angle of a part = (part ÷ total) × 360°.
concepts.analogy: A line chart is a cardiogram (how things move over time); a pie chart is a pizza (who got how big a slice).
concepts.work: Annual reports show revenue mix as a pie, five-year revenue as a bar chart and share price as a line chart. Choosing the wrong one confuses readers.

concepts.title: Frequency distribution and its terms
body: An attribute is a qualitative characteristic (gender); a variable is quantitative. A discrete variable takes isolated values (number of printing errors); a continuous variable can take any value in a range (weight).

Steps: find the range (largest − smallest); decide the class width and number of classes so that number of classes × width ≥ range (always round up); write the classes; put tally marks; count them into a frequency column; confirm the total equals the number of observations.

Class limits: the lowest (LCL) and highest (UCL) values a class can hold. Class boundaries: the true limits. In exclusive (overlapping) classes like 10–20, 20–30, boundaries equal limits, and a value equal to 20 goes to 20–30. In inclusive (non-overlapping) classes like 10–19, 20–29, LCB = LCL − D/2 and UCB = UCL + D/2, where D is the gap between the UCL of a class and the LCL of the next.

Mid-value (class mark) = (LCL + UCL) ÷ 2 = (LCB + UCB) ÷ 2. Width = UCB − LCB. Frequency density = class frequency ÷ class width. Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ total frequency (× 100 gives percentage frequency). Less-than cumulative frequency counts observations up to an upper boundary; more-than cumulative frequency counts those from a lower boundary onwards.

blocks.title: Marks of 50 students in a practice test

concepts.analogy: A frequency table is a set of labelled boxes; class boundaries are the walls between boxes, with no gap left for any value to fall through.
concepts.work: A receivables ageing schedule (0–30, 31–60, 61–90 days) is a frequency distribution of invoices by age. Auditors use it to judge the provision for doubtful debts.

concepts.title: Graphs of a frequency distribution
body: Histogram: adjacent rectangles on class boundaries; area represents frequency. With equal widths, height = frequency; with unequal widths, height = frequency density. The histogram is used to locate the mode graphically.
Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of the tops of the histogram rectangles (or plot frequency against mid-values) and close it by joining to the mid-points of an empty class at each end.

Ogives (cumulative frequency graphs): less-than ogive — less-than c.f. against upper boundaries (rises); more-than ogive — more-than c.f. against lower boundaries (falls). They intersect at N/2, and the foot of that point on the x-axis is the median. Ogives also give quartiles and short-term projections.

Frequency curve: a smooth curve through the points of the polygon. Shapes: bell-shaped (most common — heights, marks, profits); U-shaped (frequency lowest in the middle, highest at the ends); J-shaped (rises to a maximum at one end) and inverted J; mixed curves.
concepts.analogy: An ogive is a staircase of running totals; the step where half the crowd has passed is the median.
concepts.work: Credit teams chart cumulative overdue amounts to show "x% of receivables are within 60 days" — that is reading an ogive.

illustrations.title: All the frequency-distribution terms in one table
illustrations.q: Marks of 50 students: 10–19: 4, 20–29: 7, 30–39: 12, 40–49: 15, 50–59: 8, 60–69: 4. Find class boundaries, mid-values, relative frequencies, frequency densities and both cumulative frequencies.

Frequency density (f ÷ 10)
Less-than c.f. (up to UCB)
More-than c.f. (from LCB)
solution.title: Marks of 50 students in a practice test
Working notes
solution.text: Gap between 19 and 20 is 1, so D/2 = 0.5: each class becomes LCL − 0.5 to UCL + 0.5; width = 10. Mid-value of 10–19 = (10 + 19) ÷ 2 = 14.5. Relative frequency of 40–49 = 15 ÷ 50 = 0.3. Less-than c.f. at 39.5 = 4 + 7 + 12 = 23. More-than c.f. from 29.5 = 50 − 4 − 7 = 39.
Read the less-than column against the upper boundary (e.g. 23 students scored below 39.5) and the more-than column against the lower boundary (e.g. 39 students scored 29.5 or more).

illustrations.title: Angles for a pie chart
illustrations.q: Of every ₹120 lakh of sales, Neelgiri Foods spends ₹48 lakh on raw material, ₹30 lakh on wages, ₹18 lakh on power and fuel and ₹12 lakh on administration; profit is ₹12 lakh. Compute the angles for a pie chart.

solution.title: How each ₹120 lakh of sales revenue of Neelgiri Foods is used
Rule
solution.text: Angle = item ÷ total × 360. Raw material: 48 ÷ 120 × 360 = 144°. The angles must add up to 360°.

illustrations.title: Choosing and preparing a percentage bar diagram
illustrations.q: Sales (₹ lakh) of products A, B and C were 60, 90, 50 in 2025 and 84, 105, 61 in 2026. Management wants to compare the product mix of the two years. Which diagram suits, and what figures are plotted?

solution.text: Because totals differ (₹200 lakh vs ₹250 lakh) and the question is about mix, a percentage (divided) bar diagram is best: two bars of equal height (100%), each divided into A, B and C. Two pie charts would also work. A component bar in absolute ₹ would show growth, not mix.

solution.title: Shares
solution.text: A: 60 ÷ 200 = 30% → 84 ÷ 250 = 33.6%. B: 45% → 42%. C: 25% → 24.4%. Product A gained share even though all three grew in value.

illustrations.title: Histogram with unequal class widths
illustrations.q: Invoices by days outstanding: 0–10: 5, 10–20: 12, 20–40: 24, 40–70: 18, 70–100: 6. What heights should the histogram bars have?

solution.text: With unequal widths the area — not the height — must represent frequency, so heights are frequency densities (f ÷ width). Taking 10 days as the standard width, the 20–40 bar is 24 ÷ 20 × 10 = 12 units tall, not 24. Plotting raw frequencies would make the wide classes look far bigger than they are.

jobs.title: Turning a debtors list into an ageing distribution
jobs.role: Articled assistant, statutory audit of a distributor
jobs.situation: The client gives you a list of 1,240 open invoices with dates. Your senior wants an ageing summary (0–30, 31–60, 61–90, 91–180, over 180 days) and a chart for the audit committee.
steps: Compute the days outstanding for each invoice at the year-end date (a discrete variable — whole days).
Use inclusive classes (0–30, 31–60 …) because days are whole numbers; note that the true boundaries are 30.5, 60.5 and so on.
Count invoices and amounts in each class; check that both totals agree with the ledger (scrutiny / internal consistency).
Add a percentage column and a less-than cumulative percentage column ("82% of the amount is within 90 days").
Because the last class is open-ended and widths differ, present a table plus a bar chart of amounts rather than a histogram.
jobs.takeaway: An ageing schedule is just a frequency distribution of receivables. The totals check and the cumulative column are what make it useful evidence.
jobs.think: Why would a histogram of invoice counts drawn with raw frequencies mislead if the class 91–180 is three times as wide as 61–90?
jobs.answer: Area would overstate the wide class threefold. Heights must be frequency densities (count ÷ width) for a histogram with unequal widths.

jobs.title: Picking the right chart for a management deck
jobs.role: Finance executive in a listed FMCG company
jobs.situation: You must show (a) the cost structure of every ₹100 of sales, (b) eight years of revenue that grew from ₹40 crore to ₹900 crore, and (c) revenue by State.
steps: (a) Parts of a whole → pie chart or a percentage bar; compute angles as share × 360°.
(b) Huge range and interest in growth rates → a ratio (log) line chart, so equal growth rates show as equal slopes.
(c) Spatial, qualitative categories → horizontal bar diagram, sorted by size.
Put the supporting table with exact figures in the appendix — diagrams are attractive but less accurate.
jobs.takeaway: The type of data decides the diagram: time → line, categories/places → horizontal bars, parts of a whole → pie or percentage bar.
jobs.think: On an ordinary line chart, would growth from ₹40 crore to ₹80 crore look as important as growth from ₹450 crore to ₹900 crore?
jobs.answer: No — both are 100% growth, but on a natural scale the second rise looks ten times bigger. A ratio (log) chart shows both as equal slopes.

mcqs.q: Statistics used in the plural sense means:
options: Numerical data collected with a view to analysis
The science of collecting and analysing data
A single figure such as an average
Only data published by the government
mcqs.explain: Plural sense = the figures themselves. The singular sense is the method (science) of collecting, analysing and presenting data.

mcqs.q: In the singular sense, statistics is best described as:
options: The scientific method of collecting, analysing and presenting data and drawing inferences
A set of numbers about a characteristic
mcqs.explain: As a singular noun, statistics is the method or science; as a plural noun it means data.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a limitation of statistics?
options: It cannot be used in economics
mcqs.explain: Statistics deals with aggregates; a single item has no importance except as part of the group.

mcqs.q: Data collected by an investigator for the first time for his own enquiry are called:
mcqs.explain: First-hand, original collection gives primary data. Later users of those data treat them as secondary.

mcqs.q: Which method of collecting primary data usually suffers the highest non-response?
mcqs.explain: Many recipients never return a mailed questionnaire, so non-response is highest there.

mcqs.q: After a train accident the injured cannot be reached, so information is collected from relatives and railway staff. This is:
mcqs.explain: When respondents cannot be approached directly, data are collected from persons connected with the problem — indirect interview.

mcqs.q: The method that is quick and cheap with wide coverage, but less consistent, is the:
mcqs.explain: Telephone interviews cover a wide area quickly and at low cost; personal and indirect interviews are more accurate but cannot cover a large area.

mcqs.q: Measuring the heights of students directly is an example of:
options: Observation method — reliable but slow and limited in coverage
mcqs.explain: Direct measurement is observation. It is probably the best method for accuracy, but it is time-consuming and covers only a small area.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a source of secondary data?
options: A report published by the World Bank
Your own measurement of machine output
mcqs.explain: International bodies, government publications and research institutes are standard secondary sources.

mcqs.q: Checking whether Density = Population ÷ Area holds for the data of several towns is a part of:
mcqs.explain: Related series can be tested against each other for internal consistency during scrutiny.

mcqs.q: Data on CA Foundation candidates arranged State-wise are:
mcqs.explain: Arrangement by region or place gives geographical (spatial) series.

mcqs.q: Which pair belongs to the non-frequency group of data?
options: Time series data and geographical data
mcqs.explain: Qualitative and quantitative data are counted into groups (frequency data); time series and geographical data are not.

mcqs.q: Data on the smoking habits of a group of people are:
mcqs.explain: Smoking habit is an attribute, so classifying by it gives qualitative (ordinal) data.

mcqs.q: In a statistical table, the stub is:
options: The left part of the table describing the rows
The upper part describing the columns
The main part containing the figures
The note at the bottom of the table
mcqs.explain: Stub = row descriptions (left). Caption = column headings (top). Body = figures. Footnote/source = bottom.

mcqs.q: In tabulation, the caption refers to:
options: The headings of the columns and sub-columns
mcqs.explain: The caption describes the columns; the box-head is the whole upper part including the caption, column numbers and units.

mcqs.q: Compared with tabulation, diagrammatic representation is:
options: Both more accurate and more attractive
Of no use to a lay reader
mcqs.explain: Diagrams appeal to everyone and reveal trends, but when accuracy is the priority a table is recommended.

mcqs.q: In a pie chart of total expenses of ₹1,20,000, rent of ₹27,000 is shown by an angle of:
mcqs.explain: Angle = 27,000 ÷ 1,20,000 × 360 = 81 degrees degrees. (27 is just the amount in thousands; 22.5 is the percentage.)

mcqs.q: For a time series whose values range from very small to very large, and where the rate of growth matters, the most suitable diagram is:
mcqs.explain: In a ratio chart the log of the value is plotted, so equal rates of change appear as equal slopes.

mcqs.q: Horizontal bar diagrams are generally used for:
options: Qualitative data or data varying over space
mcqs.explain: Horizontal bars suit categories and places; vertical bars suit quantitative and time series data.

mcqs.q: To compare the components of a total and also show each as a share of the whole, one may use:
options: A percentage (divided) bar diagram or a pie chart
mcqs.explain: Percentage bars and pie charts both show parts in relation to the whole.

mcqs.q: For the inclusive classes 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, the lower class boundary of 30–39 is:
A class has boundaries 24.5 and 34.5. Its mid-value is:
mcqs.explain: Mid-value = (24.5 + 34.5) ÷ 2 = 29.5. (10 is the width.)

mcqs.q: In a distribution of 120 items, a class has frequency 18. Its relative frequency is:
mcqs.explain: Relative frequency = 18 ÷ 120 = 0.15 (i.e. 15% when expressed as a percentage).

mcqs.q: The class 20–40 has frequency 24. Its frequency density is:
mcqs.explain: Frequency density = frequency ÷ width = 24 ÷ 20 = 1.2.

mcqs.q: Frequencies of the classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 are 5, 9, 14, 7. The more-than cumulative frequency corresponding to 20 is:
mcqs.explain: More-than c.f. at 20 counts all items in 20–30 and 30–40: 14 + 7 = 21. (28 is the less-than c.f. at 30.)

mcqs.q: The largest observation is 82 and the smallest is 24. With a class width of 8, the number of classes needed is:
mcqs.explain: Range = 58; classes × 8 must be at least 58, so 58 ÷ 8 = 7.25 is rounded up to 8. Seven classes would leave the extreme values out.

mcqs.q: With exclusive classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40, an observation of exactly 20 is placed in:
mcqs.explain: In exclusive (overlapping) classes the upper limit is excluded, so 20 belongs to 20–30.

mcqs.q: The number of children in a family is an example of:
mcqs.explain: It can take only whole-number values, so it is discrete.

mcqs.q: The point where the less-than and more-than ogives intersect gives the:
mcqs.explain: They cross at N/2, so the x-value of that point is the median.

mcqs.q: A histogram is used to find which measure graphically?
mcqs.explain: The mode is located from the tallest rectangle of the histogram; ogives give the median and quartiles.

mcqs.q: A frequency polygon is obtained by joining:
options: The mid-points of the tops of histogram rectangles
The upper corners of histogram rectangles
mcqs.explain: Plot frequency against mid-values (the mid-tops of the rectangles) and close the figure at both ends.

mcqs.q: In a histogram with unequal class widths, the heights of the rectangles should be proportional to:
mcqs.explain: Area must represent frequency, so height = frequency ÷ width.

mcqs.q: A frequency curve in which frequency is lowest in the middle and highest at both ends is:
mcqs.explain: U-shaped: minimum near the centre, rising towards both extremes.

mcqs.q: Most distributions of heights, weights and marks give a:
mcqs.explain: Frequencies start low, rise to a peak and fall again — the familiar bell shape.

questions.q: Ages (years) of 30 employees of Vardhan Logistics: 23, 37, 41, 28, 33, 45, 26, 39, 31, 48, 22, 35, 29, 44, 36, 27, 40, 34, 38, 25, 42, 30, 47, 32, 36, 24, 43, 39, 33, 29. Construct a frequency distribution with exclusive classes of width 5 starting at 20. Show the range, the number of classes and tally marks.

model.title: Step 1 — range and classes
model.text: Range = 48 − 22 = 26. Number of classes × 5 ≥ 26, so number of classes = next integer of 26 ÷ 5 = 6. Starting at 20: 20–25, 25–30, …, 45–50.

Tally marks
No. of employees
model.title: Ages of 30 employees of Vardhan Logistics
Step 3 — check

Several candidates forget to show the total and therefore miss a tallying error.
tips: Tick each raw value as you tally it.
Always end with a total row and compare it with n.

questions.q: A family spends its monthly income as follows: food ₹13,500, rent ₹9,000, education ₹6,000, transport ₹3,600 and savings ₹3,900. Compute the angles to draw a pie chart.

scheme.pt: All five angles correct and adding to 360°

remarks: Good answers show the formula once and then a table.
Weak answers give percentages and stop.

questions.q: Daily units sold by a dealer over 60 days: 100–199: 6, 200–299: 14, 300–399: 22, 400–499: 12, 500–599: 6. (a) Find class boundaries and mid-values. (b) Prepare less-than and more-than cumulative frequencies. (c) If both ogives are drawn, at what cumulative frequency do they meet, and in which class does that point lie?

model.title: (a)
model.text: Gap between 199 and 200 is 1, so subtract 0.5 from lower limits and add 0.5 to upper limits; width = 100. Mid-value of 100–199 = 149.5.

model.title: (c)
model.text: The ogives meet at N/2 = 30. Less-than c.f. is 20 at 299.5 and 42 at 399.5, so the 30th value lies in 299.5–399.5 (class 300–399). The x-value of the meeting point is the median.

scheme.pt: Meeting point at N/2 = 30 and class 300–399 identified

remarks: Many candidates plot the less-than c.f. against lower boundaries — it belongs at upper boundaries.
The idea that ogives cross at N/2 is tested often in MCQs.
mistakes: Using class limits instead of boundaries for ogives.
Writing the more-than c.f. in the wrong order.
tips: Less-than goes with UCB, more-than goes with LCB.
Both cumulative columns end at N — use that as a check.

checks.label: N/2, where the two ogives cross

summary: Statistics: plural = data; singular = science of collecting, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.
Limitations: aggregates only, quantitative only, conditional projections, needs random samples.
Primary (first-hand) vs secondary (reused). Primary methods: interview (personal, indirect, telephone), mailed questionnaire, observation, enumerators.
Table parts: number, title, caption/box-head, stub, body, footnote, source.
Diagrams: line/historiagram, ratio (log) chart, bar diagrams (horizontal, vertical, multiple, component, percentage), pie chart.
Frequency terms: limits, boundaries, mid-value, width, density, relative and cumulative frequency.
Graphs: histogram (mode), frequency polygon, ogives (median, quartiles), frequency curves (bell, U, J).
remember: Inclusive classes: LCB = LCL − D/2, UCB = UCL + D/2.
Number of classes = range ÷ width, rounded UP.
traps: Stub (rows) vs caption (columns) — do not swap them.
Unequal widths: histogram heights are densities, not frequencies.
Time series and geographical data are non-frequency data.
Exclusive classes: the upper limit belongs to the next class.

quickref.v: LCB = LCL − D/2; UCB = UCL + D/2 (D = gap between UCL and next LCL)
Class frequency ÷ total frequency (× 100 = percentage frequency)
Less-than: c.f. vs UCB (rising); more-than: c.f. vs LCB (falling); meet at N/2 → median

viva.q: What is the difference between primary data and secondary data?
viva.model: Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator himself for his own purpose, so they are original. Secondary data are data that were already collected by someone else and are only used by the investigator, for example from published government reports. The same data are primary for the one who collected them and secondary for anyone who later uses them.

viva.q: What are the main parts of a statistical table?
viva.model: A table has a table number and a clear title. The caption gives the headings of the columns, and the box-head is the whole upper part with the column headings and units. The stub is the left part that describes the rows. The body holds the figures. Footnotes and the source note come at the bottom.

points.pt: Table number and title
Caption / box-head: column headings
kw: caption column|caption heading|caption top|caption upper|box head column|box head heading|box head top|box head upper|boxhead column|boxhead heading|boxhead top|boxhead upper

points.pt: Stub: row descriptions on the left
Body holds the figures; footnote / source at the bottom

viva.q: How do class limits differ from class boundaries, and how do you get boundaries from inclusive classes like 10 to 19?
viva.model: Class limits are the smallest and largest values written for a class, such as 10 and 19. Class boundaries are the actual limits with no gaps between classes. For inclusive classes we take half the gap between one upper limit and the next lower limit, here half of one, and subtract it from the lower limit and add it to the upper limit, so 10 to 19 becomes 9.5 to 19.5.

points.pt: Limits: the stated lowest and highest values of a class
Boundaries: actual limits with no gap between classes
Subtract half the gap from the lower limit and add it to the upper limit

viva.q: What is an ogive and what can you read from it?
viva.model: An ogive is a cumulative frequency graph. The less-than ogive plots less-than cumulative frequencies against upper class boundaries and rises; the more-than ogive plots more-than cumulative frequencies against lower class boundaries and falls. The point where the two ogives cross gives the median on the horizontal axis, and ogives can also be used to read quartiles.

points.pt: Cumulative frequency graph
Less-than ogive (upper boundaries, rising) and more-than ogive (lower boundaries, falling)
Intersection of the two ogives gives the median

viva.q: State any three limitations of statistics.
viva.model: Statistics studies aggregates, not individuals; a single item has no importance by itself. It deals with quantitative data, so qualities must first be given numbers. Projections hold only if the underlying conditions stay the same. And if the sample is not random, the conclusions can be wrong.

points.pt: Deals with aggregates, not individuals
kw: aggregate|group|mass|not individual|no individual|not with individual|individual has no

points.pt: Only quantitative data (qualities must be quantified)
Projections/inferences fail if conditions change or sample is not random

cases.title: Sales-per-shop data for a distributor
cases.case: Amrit Distributors supplies 100 retail shops. Its analyst groups the number of cartons each shop bought in October into the classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59, with 8, 20, 32, 25 and 15 shops respectively. She wants a table for the management report, an ogive to read off the middle shop, and a pie chart for the board deck.

mcqs.q: What are the class boundaries of the class 30–39?
mcqs.explain: The gap between one upper limit and the next lower limit is 1, so subtract and add half of it: 30 − 0.5 = 29.5 and 39 + 0.5 = 39.5.

mcqs.q: What is the less-than cumulative frequency at 39.5?
mcqs.explain: Less-than c.f. adds frequencies from the top: 8 + 20 + 32 = 60.

mcqs.q: If the two ogives are drawn, at what cumulative frequency will they cross?
mcqs.explain: The less-than and more-than ogives always meet at half the total frequency: 100 ÷ 2 = 50. The x-value there is the median.

mcqs.q: In the pie chart, what angle represents the shops in the class 30–39?
mcqs.explain: Angle = 32 ÷ 100 × 360 = 115.2 degrees.
